range has no Kwargs parameter, so the keyword argument lands in the next integer slot, where a map is not an integer.
dict DOES take keyword arguments; this is the valid form, not an error.
namespace has no Kwargs parameter either, but its parameter is a Value, so the keyword map lands in it and becomes the namespace.
str.join iterates its argument, so a number is an invalid operation. The port used to range over a nil slice and return an empty string.
none iterates as empty, so this joins to nothing rather than failing.
A keyword argument reaches a method as one trailing value, so this is a non-string argument rather than an ignored keyword.
The keyword map lands in the required `from` parameter: an invalid operation, not too many arguments.
Same, one slot later.
`Cow<str>` stringifies a non-string argument, so this is not an error.
`last` reaches for a sequence; a mapping is an invalid operation there, while `first` reaches for the object and accepts one.
The counterpart: `first` DOES accept a mapping and yields its first key.
Measured: reversing a mapping yields its keys in iteration order, unreversed, while `|items|reverse` does reverse.
The operand that cannot be iterated is yielded as an invalid value, in place. Dropping it would silently change the data.
Unconsumed, the chain is an iterator.
A lazy chain is an iterable, so it has no length.
Taking the invalid value out of the list is where the deferred error surfaces — at the lookup, not at the rendering. contract/invalid-item-lookup-compared is what distinguishes the two.
Through serde an invalid value is null.
none iterates as empty, so it contributes nothing rather than an invalid value.
All-sequence chaining produces a sequence, which does have a length.
False in the engine: the keyword map is one of the debugged values.
True: it is debugged as exactly that map.
A filter result is not a validation point, so the marker is what renders. Rejecting it here would be a divergence in the other direction.
An invalid value is not undefined, so `default` returns it unchanged.
An invalid value is falsy rather than an error in a condition.
Reading an attribute OFF an invalid value yields undefined: the engine validates the RESULT of a lookup, not its subject.
`last` reaches past the invalid element, so it never sees it.
The item lookup's RESULT is validated (vm/mod.rs:350-357).
Same point, one operation earlier than the render — which is what distinguishes validating at the boundary from validating at output.

rows.source: {% for x in 42|chain([1]) %}{% if x is defined %}D{% endif %}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Every item an iteration yields is validated (vm/mod.rs:479-484), so the loop fails before its body runs.
Materialising the chain first does not help: iterating the list validates its items too.
A variable lookup is a validation point (vm/mod.rs:322-326), so storing an invalid value and reading it back fails.
`int` and `float` are the two filters that reveal the error themselves (filters.rs:580, 600).
Not validation: an ordinary type error, since an invalid value is not a number.
An evaluated noncallable value is an invalid operation, not an unknown function: nothing about it is a name lookup.
A generic host object that does not implement calling.
An invalid value is not callable either, and reports its own kind.
An attribute that exists but is not callable — the method path's own spelling of the same rule.
A bare NAME that resolves to a number: resolved, so invalid operation.
A defined variable holding undefined is still RESOLVED, so this is an invalid operation while an unresolved name is an unknown function.
The one case that stays an unknown function.
The method path is separate and keeps its own class.
The argument's invalid operation, NOT `nosuchfn is unknown`: the engine has already evaluated the arguments when it resolves the name.
A keyword argument is evaluated at the same point as a positional one.
`super` is the one name handled before the lookup, and its arguments are still evaluated first.
A local shadows a DEFAULT FUNCTION, so this is a noncallable number rather than a `range` call.
A context value shadows it too.

rows.source: {% macro range() %}M{% endmacro %}{% set range = 42 %}{{ range() }}
rows.notes: A local assigned after a macro definition shadows the macro.

rows.source: {% set dict = 42 %}{% macro dict() %}M{% endmacro %}{{ dict() }}
rows.notes: And the other order: a macro definition IS a local assignment, so the one defined last wins.

rows.source: {% for x in [1] recursive %}{{ loop(1, 42|sort) }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: The argument error wins over the arity check, because the arguments are evaluated first here too.

rows.source: {% for x in [1] recursive %}{{ loop(1, 2) }}{% endfor %}

rows.notes: `loop` resolves to a loop object that was not set up for recursion.
Outside a loop the name does not resolve at all, so it is an unknown function.

rows.source: {% for x in [[1, [2]]] recursive %}{{ x[0] }}{{ loop(x[1]) }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Recursion still recurses.

rows.source: {% for x in [1] recursive %}{{ loop([2]) }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Unbounded recursion is an invalid operation on both sides.
Resolvable name, unusable context: an invalid operation, not an unknown function.

rows.source: {% for i in [1] %}{% macro x() %}M{% endmacro %}{% endfor %}{{ x() }}
rows.notes: A macro defined inside a loop body is gone when the frame pops. It used to stay callable through the template-level registry, which is a false success rather than an error-text difference.

rows.source: {% for i in [1] %}{% macro x() %}M{% endmacro %}{{ x() }}{% endfor %}
{% with %}{% macro x() %}M{% endmacro %}{% endwith %}{{ x() }}
{% with %}{% macro x() %}M{% endmacro %}{{ x() }}{% endwith %}
{% macro outer() %}{% macro inner() %}I{% endmacro %}{{ inner() }}{% endmacro %}{{ outer() }}|{{ inner() }}
rows.notes: A macro defined inside another macro dies with that macro's frame.

rows.source: {% macro outer() %}{% macro inner() %}I{% endmacro %}{{ inner() }}{% endmacro %}{{ outer() }}
{% if true %}{% macro x() %}M{% endmacro %}{% endif %}{{ x() }}
rows.notes: An `if` body is not a frame, so a macro defined there is a top-level one.

rows.source: {% if true %}{% if true %}{% macro x() %}M{% endmacro %}{% endif %}{% endif %}{{ x() }}
{% if false %}{% macro x() %}M{% endmacro %}{% endif %}{{ x() }}

rows.notes: Definition is execution, not hoisting.

rows.source: {% for i in [1, 2] %}{% macro x() %}M{{ i }}{% endmacro %}{{ x() }}{% endfor %}
{% for i in [1] %}{% macro x() %}M{% endmacro %}{% endfor %}{{ x is defined }}
{% macro x() %}T{% endmacro %}{% for i in [1] %}{% macro x() %}L{% endmacro %}{% endfor %}{{ x() }}
rows.notes: A loop-local definition must not overwrite the top-level one for good.

rows.source: {% macro f(caller) %}F{{ caller() }}{% endmacro %}{% call f() %}C{% endcall %}
{% macro f(caller) %}F{{ caller() }}{% endmacro %}{% set f = 42 %}{% call f() %}C{% endcall %}
rows.notes: A local shadows the macro for a call block exactly as it does for a call.
An unresolved callee is an unknown function, not `call block requires a macro`.
And the argument is evaluated first, so its error wins.

rows.source: {% macro f(a, caller) %}F{% endmacro %}{% call f(42|sort) %}C{% endcall %}
{% macro f(a, caller) %}{{ a }}{{ caller() }}{% endmacro %}{% call f(7) %}C{% endcall %}
{% macro f(caller) %}{{ caller(1) }}{% endmacro %}{% call(x) f() %}C{{ x }}{% endcall %}
{% for i in [1] %}{% macro f(caller) %}F{{ caller() }}{% endmacro %}{% endfor %}{% call f() %}C{% endcall %}
rows.notes: A call block sees the same lifetime as a call.

rows.source: {% for i in [1] %}{% macro f(caller) %}F{{ caller() }}{% endmacro %}{% call f() %}C{% endcall %}{% endfor %}

rows.notes: `range` has no Kwargs parameter, so the caller lands in an integer slot.
A call block on a method goes through method dispatch.

rows.source: {% macro f() %}{{ caller is defined }}{% endmacro %}{% call f() %}C{% endcall %}
rows.notes: `caller` is bound when the macro's BODY uses it, declared or not.

rows.source: {% macro f() %}F{% endmacro %}{% call f() %}C{% endcall %}
rows.notes: A macro that never mentions `caller` reports it as an unknown keyword argument.

rows.source: {% macro f() %}{{ caller() }}{% endmacro %}{% call f() %}C{% endcall %}

rows.notes: A declared parameter named caller is an ordinary parameter.
